content: 1. Individuals with persistently normal ALT levels consistently exhibit a low incidence of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) per 100 person-years. 2. A systematic review and meta-analysis aggregated data from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomized studies to estimate the efficacy of antiviral therapy in preventing clinical outcomes among individuals with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) without cirrhosis. These studies were stratified by baseline HBV DNA levels (<2000, 2000–20,000, 20,000–200,000, and ≥200,000 IU/mL) or ALT levels (<1, 1–2, and ≥2 times the upper limit of normal [ULN]). 3. A total of 43 studies (31 RCTs and 12 observational studies) met the inclusion criteria. Of these, 52% were conducted in Asia, 17% in Europe, 5% in North America, and none in Africa. 4. Half of the studies (21 studies) focused on adults aged ≥18 years, while 31% (13 studies) focused on individuals <18 years of age. 5. Most studies (86%) reported outcomes only for groups with HBV DNA >20,000 IU/mL. Only one RCT and five observational studies (14%) reported results for groups with HBV DNA <2000 IU/mL, with five studies focusing on <2000 IU/mL and one on 2000–20,000 IU/mL. 6. Antiviral therapy was associated with improved biochemical outcomes (ALT normalization) and some viral outcomes (undetectable viral load), particularly in groups with higher baseline HBV DNA levels (>20,000 IU/mL). 7. Treatment efficacy was greater at higher baseline HBV DNA levels for key clinical outcomes (e.g., HCC) and histological outcomes (e.g., fibrosis and necroinflammation). 8. The certainty of evidence supporting treatment efficacy was very low or low for lower HBV DNA strata (<2000 and 2000–20,000 IU/mL) and ranged from very low to high for higher HBV DNA strata. 9. Data for studies with HBV DNA >2 million IU/mL (2 million–20 million, 20 million–200 million, and >200 million IU/mL) were not shown. 10. Among children and adolescents (<18 years), the effectiveness of treatment based on baseline HBV DNA and ALT levels is addressed in Chapter 8. 11. The number needed to treat (NNT) for an additional beneficial outcome was estimated for each HBV DNA stratum based on natural history studies and the efficacy of antiviral therapy from systematic reviews. 12. Modeling the impact of changing hepatitis B treatment eligibility criteria across WHO regions showed that removing the ALT > ULN criterion had the greatest impact, increasing the number of individuals eligible for treatment by 75–100%. 13. Lowering the HBV DNA cut-off from ≥20,000 IU/mL to ≥2000 IU/mL was the second most impactful factor in expanding treatment eligibility. 14. Lowering the age eligibility cut-off for HBV treatment to 15 years (and also 11 years) had the greatest impact in the African and Eastern Mediterranean regions, where much of the population is younger than 18 years and CHB prevalence is higher in younger age cohorts. 15. Lowering the eligibility age for treatment also significantly reduced mother-to-child transmission, especially in the African region, due to lower levels of hepatitis B birth-dose and three-dose vaccination coverage. 16. Expanding treatment eligibility criteria modestly impacted outcomes such as HCC incidence, decompensated cirrhosis, and deaths averted, suggesting that even conservative guidelines already target those most likely to progress to advanced liver disease. 17. Updated recommendations prioritize identifying individuals who should receive treatment rather than those who should not. 18. Four new recommended options for meeting treatment eligibility criteria aim to capture a higher proportion (at least 50%) of all HBsAg-positive individuals compared to about 20% previously. 19. The flexible and inclusive approach with four options for treatment eligibility is applicable to all settings, including those with or without access to HBV DNA testing. 20. Most HBsAg-positive individuals will meet treatment criteria without requiring an HBV DNA assay, as only one of the four recommendations requires access to HBV DNA testing. 21. The recommendations apply to adults and adolescents aged 12 years or older, including those of reproductive age and pregnant women, enabling a common entry point for assessment and treatment across age groups. 22. Expanding treatment to adolescents, particularly adolescent girls of reproductive age, complements recommendations for expanded use of antiviral prophylaxis to reduce mother-to-child transmission. 23. Although only one of the four treatment eligibility criteria requires HBV DNA testing, it is strongly encouraged to perform at least one HBV DNA test if available to provide a full assessment before initiating treatment. HBV DNA levels are also required for monitoring treatment response. 24. Presenting the level of certainty of evidence (high, moderate, low, or very low) for each recommendation is important to inform discussions and shared decision-making between healthcare workers and patients. 25. The updated 2024 WHO guidelines are informed by two systematic reviews: one on the natural history of CHB infection and the other on the efficacy of antiviral therapy. 26. The first systematic review found that higher baseline HBV DNA levels were associated with a higher progression rate of clinical outcomes (e.g., HCC, cirrhosis, and liver-related mortality). HCC incidence was low in individuals with persistently normal ALT levels. 27. The second systematic review found that the magnitude of treatment benefit was highest for individuals with HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL and elevated ALT levels (>30 U/L for men and >19 U/L for women). 28. The overall certainty of evidence was assessed as moderate for adults, low to moderate for HBV DNA levels of 2000–20,000 IU/mL, and very low for HBV DNA levels of 2000–20,000 IU/mL. For adolescents, the certainty of evidence was also assessed as low. 29. Treatment benefit was greatest in individuals with cirrhosis or significant fibrosis. 30. Chapter 8 addresses treatment recommendations and considerations for adolescents and children in more detail. 31. The Guidelines Development Group prioritized initiating antiviral therapy for individuals with advanced liver disease due to their higher risk of life-threatening complications and the potential for halving disease progression with treatment. 32. Treating individuals with significant fibrosis and cirrhosis is an effective use of resources and has the greatest impact on reducing morbidity and mortality. 33. Antiviral therapy for individuals with HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL and ALT > ULN is estimated to capture 20–35% of all HBsAg-positive individuals, depending on the region. 34. Evidence indicates much higher disease progression for individuals with HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL or ALT > ULN compared to those with HBV DNA <2000 IU/mL or normal ALT levels. 35. Limited evidence suggests some benefit of antiviral therapy for individuals with HBV DNA <2000 IU/mL and normal ALT levels. 36. Including criteria such as coinfections, family history of HCC or cirrhosis, immune suppression, comorbidities, and extrahepatic manifestations for antiviral therapy will capture an estimated 5–8% of HBsAg-positive individuals. 37. HIV coinfection accelerates HBV disease progression and increases the risk of cirrhosis, HCC, and liver-related mortality. Treating HIV and HBV coinfection with ARV regimens containing TDF or TAF has substantially improved outcomes. 38. HBV and HCV coinfection increases the risk of aggressive HCC at a younger age. Treating both infections is generally required, and nucleos(t)ide analogues are recommended during and after HCV direct-acting antiviral therapy to prevent HBV reactivation. 39. Chronic HDV infection is the most aggressive form of viral hepatitis, with accelerated progression to cirrhosis or liver cancer. Novel agents for HDV treatment are showing favorable results in clinical trials. 40. The prevalence of steatotic liver disease among individuals with CHB is increasing worldwide. Metabolic dysfunction (e.g., diabetes, obesity, dyslipidemia) is a risk factor for fibrosis progression and HCC development. 41. Aggressive correction of metabolic dysfunction and earlier initiation of antiviral therapy may improve clinical outcomes, though direct evidence is lacking. 42. Immunosuppressive therapies can induce HBV reactivation, and pre-emptive antiviral use is recommended. 43. Extrahepatic manifestations of hepatitis B, such as glomerulonephritis, vasculitis, or arthritis, are rare but represent indications for antiviral therapy. 44. A conditional recommendation for treatment based on persistently abnormal ALT levels regardless of APRI score is intended for settings without HBV DNA testing. This captures an estimated 20% of HBsAg-positive individuals. 45. Other common causes of persistently abnormal ALT, such as impaired glucose tolerance or dyslipidemia, should also be considered.
